chunks: "Cycle time is pull-in time plus release time plus return stroke, so I'd attack each. Pull-in is limited by how fast current builds against the coil's inductance.
The force is proportional to current squared, so the plunger doesn't move until the current reaches a threshold.
If I drive at the rated voltage the current rises as L over R , slow.
The fix is over-excitation: apply a much higher voltage, say 3x, for the first few milliseconds, then switch to a lower holding voltage or PWM current.
In an example 24 volt solenoid, 72 volts pulls it in in about 7. 5 milliseconds instead of 19. 5 milliseconds.
Once the plunger is closed the gap is small and a quarter of the current holds it, so I chop to a hold current and cut the heating by 90%, which is also what makes the overdrive thermally okay.
Release is limited by how fast the current decays. A plain flyback diode holds the coil near zero volts so the current decays slowly.
If I put a Zener or TVS in series with the diode, say 60 volts, the coil sees minus 60 volts and the current collapses in a couple of milliseconds instead of tens.
The price is that the FET must withstand supply plus clamp.

Beyond the electronics: lighter plunger, stiffer return spring for faster release, shorter stroke, and a soft landing so the plunger doesn't bounce, because the bounce limits how soon you can fire again.
And watch the thermal budget, because overdriving heats the coil."
